revision_notes: Light check surfaced an authoritative ITU source giving a country-specific figure, so this was escalated to full verification. The ITU 'Affordability of ICT Services 2022' policy brief records Zimbabwe's data-only mobile-broadband basket (2GB) at 18.4% of GNI per capita in 2022 (down from 30.0% in 2021), well above the 10% threshold. revised_comments: The cost of a 2GB data-only mobile-broadband plan in Zimbabwe stood at 18.4% of GNI per capita in 2022, according to ITU's ICT price-basket monitoring. This is far above the UN Broadband Commission's 2% affordability target and places mobile data among the least affordable in the region, though the price has been falling steadily from 30.0% of GNI per capita in 2021.

Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced an authoritative source (Packet Clearing House IXP directory) contradicting the Unknown score, so this was escalated to full verification. PCH and PeeringDB confirm Harare IX (also known as HIXP), established November 2017 and currently active, hosted at TelOne under POTRAZ oversight. PeeringDB records only 2 registered peers/connections, though a 2020 POTRAZ contribution to the ITU African regional IXP forum states that all national Internet Access Providers are connected, and the exchange peers internationally with Packet Clearing House and Quad9. A separately listed, older 'ZINX' entry is marked defunct. Score changed from 0/Unknown to 3/Single IXP with limited participation.
revised_comments: Zimbabwe has an operational Internet Exchange Point, Harare IX (HIXP), established in November 2017 and hosted at the TelOne exchange in Harare under the oversight of the telecoms regulator, POTRAZ. The exchange peers internationally with Packet Clearing House and Quad9, and POTRAZ reports that all national Internet Access Providers are connected, though public peering databases record only a small number of registered peers. This represents a single, functioning IXP with limited participation rather than a mature, broadly-used exchange ecosystem.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching

revision_notes: Light check surfaced the national energy regulator's live tariff page, so this was escalated to full verification. ZERA (Zimbabwe Energy Regulatory Authority) currently prices the first 50 kWh lifeline block of residential electricity at USD 4.24/month. Against World Bank GNI per capita, Atlas method, of USD 2,400 in 2024 (USD 200/month), this lifeline block equates to roughly 2.1% of monthly income, i.e. the 'Moderate (2-5%)' band. Higher consumption tiers cost considerably more per kWh (USD 0.19-0.26/kWh above the lifeline block per the December 2023 approved schedule), so actual bills at typical consumption levels likely sit towards the upper end of this band. Score changed from 0/Unknown to 3, but flagged for human review because the result depends on an assumed basket size (a single lifeline block) rather than a standardised affordability index for Zimbabwe.
revised_comments: Residential electricity in Zimbabwe is priced in US dollars by the regulator, ZERA, with a lifeline block of the first 50 kWh costing around USD 4.24 per month. Relative to a GNI per capita of roughly USD 200 per month, this represents about 2% of average monthly income, placing basic electricity access in the 'moderate' affordability band, though costs rise steeply for consumption above the lifeline block.

Definition: The proportion of the population with basic digital skills (ability to use a computer, smartphone, or the internet for simple tasks such as sending messages, finding information, or using apps). Based on ITU household survey data, Afrobarometer, or national ICT surveys.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced related but non-equivalent proxies rather than a direct 'proportion of population with basic digital skills' figure, so this was escalated to full verification; no such direct percentage from ITU, Afrobarometer, or UNESCO UIS could be located for Zimbabwe. Available proxies include 50.1% of households with home internet access and 58.8% with a smartphone (ZIMSTAT/POTRAZ 2020 ICT Household Survey), and a Digital Skills Gap Index score of 4.3/10 (Wiley), above the Sub-Saharan African average of 3.4/10. None of these directly measures basic digital skills as defined by the variable, so the score is left at 0/Unknown pending a more targeted look at the ITU household ICT-skills indicator (HH15) or POTRAZ's 2025 National Digital Literacy and Digital Skills Assessment Survey, whose detailed results had not been published at the time of this check.
revised_comments: No authoritative, direct estimate of the proportion of the Zimbabwean population with basic digital skills is publicly available. Related indicators suggest partial but incomplete digital access and literacy: around half of households report home internet access and just under 60% own a smartphone, while an independent digital-skills index rates Zimbabwe modestly above the Sub-Saharan African average. POTRAZ conducted a dedicated National Digital Literacy and Digital Skills Assessment Survey, disseminated in August 2025, but detailed results were not available at the time of this review.

revision_notes: Light check surfaced academic and UNESCO sources with relevant figures, so this was escalated to full verification. Zimbabwe has several established universities offering ICT/STEM programmes, including the University of Zimbabwe, the National University of Science and Technology (Bulawayo), Midlands State University, Chinhoyi University of Technology and the dedicated Harare Institute of Technology. However, published research citing Ministry of Higher and Tertiary Education, Science and Technology Development data estimates that less than 17% of total university enrolment is in STEM-related disciplines, within an overall tertiary gross enrolment ratio of only about 9.7% (UNESCO, 2020) — both comparatively low. This is consistent with 'Moderate' rather than 'Good' or 'Strong' provision under the variable's scale. Score changed from 0/Unknown to 3.
revised_comments: Zimbabwe has several established public universities offering computer science, engineering and other STEM/ICT degree programmes, including the University of Zimbabwe, the National University of Science and Technology in Bulawayo, Midlands State University, Chinhoyi University of Technology, and the dedicated Harare Institute of Technology. Nonetheless, STEM enrolment remains a minority of total university intake at under 17%, and overall tertiary gross enrolment is low at around 9.7% of the eligible age group, reflecting capacity and access constraints rather than an absence of quality institutions.
